title: 10 Free UNSSC Online Courses 2026: Study Climate Action, Sustainability, Peace and Security Online
summary: The United Nations System Staff College has announced a collection of 10 free and open online learning opportunities for 2026, giving learners worldwide access to practical knowledge on sustainable development, digital transformation, climate action, disaster risk reduction, human security, youth participation, safe engagement with the United Nations, and the protection of children affected by armed conflict. The United Nations System Staff College, commonly known as UNSSC, shared the courses to mark International Youth Day 2026 and highlight how accessible learning can help young people and other stakeholders turn their aspirations into meaningful action. All 10 learning opportunities are delivered online and free of charge. Most are self-paced, allowing learners to access the materials and complete the required activities according to their schedules. The courses range from short two-hour learning challenges to a 12-hour digital sustainability learning path. The courses are open to international participants, although the target audience differs by course. Some programmes are designed for everyone, while others have particular relevance for young leaders, public officials, United Nations personnel, government representatives, civil society organisations, academics, marketing professionals, policymakers or practitioners working in climate action, peacebuilding and sustainable development. Most importantly, the official 2026 course pages confirm that enrolment remains open until either December 30 or December 31, 2026, depending on the course. These are genuine enrolment deadlines, and learners should register and complete the relevant requirements before access to the 2026 course cycle ends. Free UNSSC Online Courses 2026 at a Glance No. Course Duration Enrolment deadline Cost 1 Digital4Sustainability Learning Path 12 hours December 31, 2026 Free 2 Youth, Peace and Security Primer 7 hours December 30, 2026 Free 3 Youth, Peace and Security Primer on In-country Implementation 5 hours December 30, 2026 Free 4 Sustainable Lifestyles 3 hours December 31, 2026 Free 5 Human Security: From Principles to Practice Self-paced December 30, 2026 Free 6 Synergizing Disaster Risk Reduction and Climate Action Learning Path 3 hours December 31, 2026 Free 7 Systems Change x Behavioural Science for Climate Action 3.5 hours of core content December 31, 2026 Free 8 Green Marketing Challenge 2 hours December 31, 2026 Free 9 Engaging Safely at the UN 2.5 hours December 30, 2026 Free 10 Children and Armed Conflict Primer Self-paced December 30, 2026 Free Are These Courses Still Open? Yes. As of August 2026, all 10 official course pages show active 2026 course cycles. The confirmed deadlines are: Courses closing on December 30, 2026 Youth, Peace and Security Primer; Youth, Peace and Security Primer on In-country Implementation; Human Security: From Principles to Practice; Engaging Safely at the UN; and Children and Armed Conflict Primer. Courses closing on December 31, 2026 Digital4Sustainability Learning Path; Sustainable Lifestyles; Synergizing Disaster Risk Reduction and Climate Action Learning Path; Systems Change x Behavioural Science for Climate Action; and Green Marketing Challenge. The published dates should be treated as enrolment deadlines. Learners should not wait until the final day because they may need to create an account, verify their email address and access a separate learning platform. About the United Nations System Staff College The United Nations System Staff College is the learning organisation of the United Nations system. It develops and delivers learning programmes designed to strengthen the knowledge, skills and capabilities required to address complex international challenges. Its learning portfolio covers areas such as: Sustainable development and the Sustainable Development Goals; Climate and environmental action; Peace and security; Human rights; Leadership and management; Stakeholder engagement; Youth participation; Digital transformation; Change and innovation; and United Nations policy and programming. Although UNSSC was created to support learning across the United Nations system, many of its online courses are available to external participants, including government officials, civil society representatives, academics, private-sector professionals, young leaders and members of the public. Benefits of the Free UNSSC Courses These learning opportunities offer several important benefits. Free international learning No participation fee is charged for any of the 10 courses covered in this article. Fully online delivery Participants can access the programmes remotely without travelling to a UNSSC campus. Flexible, self-paced study Most courses allow learners to set their own study schedules and progress through the materials asynchronously. Exposure to United Nations frameworks The courses introduce learners to internationally recognised frameworks, including: The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development; The Sustainable Development Goals; The Paris Agreement; The Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction; UN Security Council Resolution 2250 on Youth, Peace and Security; The human security approach; The Children and Armed Conflict agenda; and United Nations standards for safe and inclusive participation. Practical and applied learning Several courses include case studies, interactive exercises, quizzes, scenarios, action-planning templates or other applied activities. Diverse subject coverage The collection is not limited to one professional field. Learners can explore technology, sustainability, climate action, peacebuilding, marketing, public policy, behavioural science, disaster risk reduction, youth participation or human rights. 1. Digital4Sustainability Learning Path The Digital4Sustainability Learning Path examines how digital transformation can support environmental and social sustainability while also addressing the environmental risks created by digital technologies. The programme was developed by UNSSC and the United Nations Environment Programme in collaboration with the German development agency GIZ, the European Union, the Coalition for Digital Environmental Sustainability and the Office of the UN Secretary-General’s Envoy on Technology. Its content is inspired by the Coalition for Digital Environmental Sustainability Action Plan for a Sustainable Planet in the Digital Age. What participants will learn The learning path helps participants understand: Digitalisation and digital transformation; Digital sustainability; The relationship between technology and sustainable development; How digital solutions can help address climate change; The role of digital tools in biodiversity conservation; How technology can support pollution prevention; Negative environmental and social effects of digital transformation; Strategies for reducing the adverse impact of digital technologies; and Systems-thinking approaches to digital sustainability. Course structure The learning path contains four modules: Digital Transformation for Sustainable Development; Digital Sustainability for Climate Action; Digital Sustainability for Biodiversity Action; and Digital Sustainability for Pollution Action. Each module takes approximately three to four hours. The entire learning path has an estimated duration of 12 hours. Who should take this course? It is suitable for anyone interested in the relationship between technology and sustainable development, including: Sustainability professionals; Technology professionals; Policymakers; Public officials; Students; Researchers; Climate practitioners; Environmental organisations; Digital-governance professionals; and Young leaders. Course deadline Enrolment closes on December 31, 2026. Access the Digital4Sustainability Learning Path 2. Youth, Peace and Security Primer The Youth, Peace and Security Primer establishes a shared understanding of the international Youth, Peace and Security Agenda and how it can be implemented by the United Nations and its partners. The course is grounded in UN Security Council Resolution 2250 and subsequent resolutions calling for the meaningful and inclusive participation of young people in peacebuilding, conflict prevention and decision-making. It was developed by UNSSC in partnership with the Folke Bernadotte Academy and builds on the Youth, Peace and Security Programming Handbook. Course contents The primer contains three foundational modules: Introduction to the Youth, Peace and Security Agenda; Enabling Meaningful Youth Participation; and Conducting Youth-Sensitive Conflict Analysis. What participants will learn Participants will develop an understanding of: The origins and principles of the Youth, Peace and Security Agenda; The importance of meaningful youth participation; The role of young people in conflict prevention and peacebuilding; Inclusive approaches to youth engagement; Youth-sensitive conflict analysis; and How institutions can work with and for young people in peace and security. Target audience The course is open to practitioners, including: Young peacebuilders; Youth leaders; UN personnel; Government officials; Civil society representatives; Academics; Peace and security practitioners; and Professionals designing youth-related programmes. Languages The programme is available in English. UNSSC’s International Youth Day announcement also identifies versions in French, Spanish, Portuguese, Georgian and Arabic. Duration and deadline The course requires approximately seven hours. Enrolment closes on December 30, 2026. Access the Youth, Peace and Security Primer 3. Youth, Peace and Security Primer on In-country Implementation The Youth, Peace and Security Primer on In-country Implementation moves beyond introducing the Youth, Peace and Security Agenda and focuses on translating it into policies, plans and coordinated action at the country level. It examines pathways for planning, implementation, monitoring and follow-up. It also introduces the institutional capabilities, stakeholder relationships and resources required for successful national implementation. The primer was developed by UNSSC in partnership with the Folke Bernadotte Academy. It builds on the 2022 guide, “Implementing the Youth, Peace and Security Agenda at Country-level: A Guide for Public Officials,” developed by the Global Coalition on Youth, Peace and Security. Learning objectives After completing the course, participants should be able to: Recognise meaningful youth participation as a foundation for national implementation; Conduct or understand contextual analysis through a youth lens; Review political commitments, laws and policies relevant to the Youth, Peace and Security Agenda; Assess institutional capacity; Map stakeholders involved in national coordination; Identify practical implementation pathways; and Develop a personal action plan for advancing the agenda. Course modules The five learning sessions cover: Introduction to the Youth, Peace and Security Agenda; A crash course on country-level implementation; Analysing, assessing and mapping; Four pathways to implementation; and Capacity, coordination and resources. Participants also receive a Personal Youth, Peace and Security Action Plan template. Target audience This course is particularly relevant to: Public officials; Young leaders; International actors; UN staff; Government representatives; Civil society practitioners; Academics; and Professionals working on national Youth, Peace and Security implementation. Languages In addition to English, the International Youth Day announcement identifies French, Spanish, Portuguese and Arabic versions. Duration and deadline The course takes approximately five hours. Enrolment closes on December 30, 2026. Access the Youth, Peace and Security Primer on In-country Implementation 4. Sustainable Lifestyles The Sustainable Lifestyles course explores how daily choices, behaviours and consumption patterns affect environmental sustainability and the achievement of the 2030 Agenda. It recognises that living patterns vary between countries, communities and social groups. Consequently, there is no single sustainable lifestyle model that can be applied universally. Instead, policies and initiatives must be adapted to different realities. Learning objectives Participants will learn to: Understand the concept of sustainable lifestyles; Recognise the collective impact of individual choices; Identify values and factors influencing lifestyle decisions; Understand major areas of consumption; Explore ways to make consumption more sustainable; Examine policy environments that support sustainable choices; Recognise how personal action can contribute to broader change; and Adapt sustainability solutions to different contexts. Course contents The programme contains four lessons: Why are we living in unsustainable ways? What are sustainable lifestyles? How can we drive lasting change? Sustainable lifestyles in action. The course combines self-paced study with case studies and interactive exercises. It presents practical examples from different sectors and regions and encourages learners to adapt relevant initiatives within their communities. Target audience The course is intended for all stakeholders interested in shaping decisions and environments that promote sustainable living. It may be particularly valuable for: Sustainability practitioners; Environmental professionals; Policymakers; Public officials; Educators; Students; Community leaders; Civil society organisations; Consumer advocates; and Members of the public seeking to reduce their environmental footprint. Duration and deadline The course takes approximately three hours. Enrolment closes on December 31, 2026. Access the Sustainable Lifestyles course 5. Human Security: From Principles to Practice Human Security: From Principles to Practice explains how the human security approach can be used to develop integrated, people-centred policies and programmes. Human security places the survival, livelihood and dignity of people at the centre of peace and development. It provides a framework for addressing interconnected challenges in a comprehensive, context-specific and prevention-oriented manner. The course examines challenges such as: Persistent poverty; Inequality; Climate change; Humanitarian crises; Transitions from emergency response to long-term development; Migration; Displacement; and Health emergencies. Learning objectives Participants will learn to: Understand the concept and operational principles of human security; Recognise the value of the human security framework; Apply human security principles when designing policies and programmes; Undertake localised and disaggregated analysis; Map needs, vulnerabilities and capacities; Develop integrated protection and empowerment strategies; Promote early action; Reduce vulnerability; Strengthen resilience; and Apply lessons from the UN Trust Fund for Human Security. Course structure The course contains six modules: Understanding the human security approach; Getting started with human security programming; Analysing complex challenges through a human security lens; Mapping needs, vulnerabilities and capacities; Designing a human security programme; and Implementing a human security programme. Target audience The course is designed for: UN personnel; Government representatives; Non-governmental organisations; Private-sector representatives; Civil society practitioners; Academics; Development professionals; and Anyone seeking to use human security in policy and programme design. Languages The course is available in English, Arabic, French and Spanish. Duration and deadline It is a self-paced course. Enrolment closes on December 30, 2026. Access Human Security: From Principles to Practice 6. Synergizing Disaster Risk Reduction and Climate Action Learning Path This updated and expanded learning path examines how disaster risk reduction and climate action can be integrated to improve resilience and make better use of resources. It was developed by UNSSC in partnership with the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction. Disaster risk reduction and climate change adaptation seek to reduce vulnerability, manage risks and strengthen resilience. However, national disaster risk reduction strategies and climate adaptation plans are often developed separately. This can result in fragmented governance, duplication and missed opportunities. The course introduces Comprehensive Risk Management as a framework for creating stronger coherence between these areas. International frameworks covered The learning path connects its subject matter to: The Paris Agreement; The Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction; The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development; and Sustainable Development Goal 13 on Climate Action. Learning objectives Participants will learn to: Explain the relationship between disaster risk reduction and climate change adaptation; Understand Comprehensive Risk Management; Identify policy and institutional mechanisms that support integration; Recognise good practices; Analyse real examples from different governance levels; Identify practical implementation pathways; Improve resource use; Strengthen resilience; and Promote more coherent risk-management strategies. Course modules The learning path contains: Promoting Coherence between Disaster Risk Reduction and Climate Change Adaptation; and Implementation Pathways for Coherent Disaster Risk Reduction and Climate Action. Target audience The course is particularly relevant to: Decision-makers; Policymakers; Disaster risk reduction focal points; Climate adaptation focal points; Professionals developing national disaster risk reduction strategies; Professionals involved in national adaptation planning; Local and subnational officials; International development practitioners; and Stakeholders supporting resilient, risk-informed development. Languages The current course is in English. UNSSC states that Spanish and French versions are expected to become available. Duration and deadline The official course page lists a duration of approximately three hours. Enrolment closes on December 31, 2026. Access the Synergizing Disaster Risk Reduction and Climate Action Learning Path 7. Systems Change x Behavioural Science for Climate Action Systems Change x Behavioural Science for Climate Action equips current and aspiring climate leaders with tools for analysing complex systems, influencing behaviour and designing scalable climate solutions. The course was developed by the UNFCCC Youth4Capacity programme with support from the Italian Ministry of Environment and Energy Security and UNSSC. It recognises that climate change cannot be addressed only through technological solutions. Effective action also requires understanding the systems, behaviours, decisions, institutions and social norms that contribute to environmental outcomes. Why systems thinking and behavioural science matter Systems thinking helps participants: Examine relationships between different parts of a system; Identify underlying causes; Understand feedback loops and patterns; Move beyond treating isolated symptoms; and Design structural interventions. Behavioural science helps participants: Understand how people make decisions; Analyse social norms; Identify barriers to action; Design initiatives that influence behaviour; and Improve the effectiveness of climate programmes. Course modules The course includes: Understanding Climate Change: People, Patterns and Systems; Systems Change for Climate Action; and Behavioural Science for Climate Action. Duration The core learning materials take approximately 3.5 hours. Participants who apply the exercises fully to their own projects may require six to eight hours. Certificate Participants who complete the three modules, mandatory quiz and evaluation form will receive a certificate. Target audience The course is open to people actively engaged or aspiring to engage in climate action. It is especially relevant to: Young people aged 18–35; Youth-led climate initiatives; UNFCCC Youth4Capacity participants; Climate Catalysts Mentorship Programme participants; Climate activists; Sustainability professionals; Project designers; Community organisers; and Emerging climate leaders. Deadline Enrolment closes on December 31, 2026. Access Systems Change x Behavioural Science for Climate Action 8. Green Marketing Challenge The Green Marketing Challenge is an interactive learning programme examining what makes a credible product sustainability claim. As consumer interest in environmentally responsible products grows, companies increasingly use green claims to promote their goods and services. However, some claims may be unclear, unsupported, exaggerated or misleading. This creates the risk of greenwashing and makes it difficult for consumers to make informed decisions. The challenge is based on the Guidelines for Providing Product Sustainability Information developed by the United Nations Environment Programme and the International Trade Centre. Learning objectives Participants will learn to: Recognise credible sustainability claims; Distinguish stronger claims from misleading claims; Understand principles for quality sustainability information; Improve environmental marketing communication; Apply 10 principles of sustainable product claims; Identify barriers to credible sustainability labelling; Support informed consumption decisions; and Reduce greenwashing risks. Course methodology Participants respond to challenges based on practical examples of good and poor sustainability claims. The programme provides feedback explaining how each example relates to international guidance. Target audience The challenge is particularly relevant to: Marketing managers; Business managers; Small and medium-sized companies; Product managers; Sustainability and ESG professionals; Civil society organisations; Consumer-protection organisations; Labelling and standards bodies; Government regulators; Communications professionals; and Consumers. Languages The programme is available in English, and UNSSC’s announcement also identifies a Spanish version. Duration and deadline The challenge takes approximately two hours. Enrolment closes on December 31, 2026. Access the Green Marketing Challenge 9. Engaging Safely at the UN Engaging Safely at the UN is a youth-focused course designed to promote safe and inclusive participation in United Nations events, meetings, conferences, working groups and intergovernmental or multi-stakeholder processes. The course was developed by the UN Youth Office with contributions from young people, civil society and United Nations partners. It responds to the fact that increasing numbers of young people are engaging with the United Nations, while acknowledging that participants may encounter harmful conduct. Issues covered The course addresses: Abuse of authority; Discrimination; Harassment; Sexual harassment; Sexual exploitation and abuse; Age-related power imbalances; Reporting mechanisms; Bystander intervention; and The UN’s responsibilities in preventing and responding to harm. Learning objectives Participants will learn to: Recognise harmful or unwelcome conduct; Understand relevant terminology; Identify available UN reporting mechanisms; Explore official and informal response options; Understand bystander intervention; Anticipate challenges; Respond more safely to difficult situations; and Understand institutional responsibilities. Course modules The five modules are: Key terms and definitions; Harassment, discrimination and abuse; Making a complaint; Anticipating and dealing with challenges; and Conclusions. The course includes quizzes, case scenarios and a reflective journal. Target audience This training is primarily designed for young people engaging with the United Nations through: Conferences; Events; Meetings; Working groups; Intergovernmental processes; Multi-stakeholder processes; and Activities at UN locations. Languages The course is available in English, French, Spanish and Arabic. Duration and deadline It takes approximately 2.5 hours. Enrolment closes on December 30, 2026. Access Engaging Safely at the UN 10. Children and Armed Conflict Primer The Children and Armed Conflict Primer introduces the United Nations Children and Armed Conflict Agenda and helps participants incorporate its principles into their professional work. The international mandate emerged following the publication of Graça Machel’s 1996 report on the impact of armed conflict on children. The report highlighted the disproportionate effect of war on children and helped establish children affected by armed conflict as an international peace and security priority. The course was developed by the Office of the Special Representative of the UN Secretary-General for Children and Armed Conflict and UNSSC. Course contents The primer contains four foundational modules: Introduction to the Children and Armed Conflict Agenda; The six grave violations against children in armed conflict; Key actors, partners and their roles; and The Children and Armed Conflict toolbox. What participants will learn Participants will develop foundational knowledge of: The origins of the Children and Armed Conflict Agenda; The impact of conflict on children; The six grave violations; Relevant international actors and institutional responsibilities; Partnerships supporting the agenda; Available tools and mechanisms; and Ways to mainstream protection considerations into professional activities. Target audience The course is open to all but is particularly relevant to: UN staff; Government representatives; Regional organisations; Civil society organisations; Academics; Peace and security professionals; Child-protection practitioners; Humanitarian workers; and Development professionals. Languages The course is available in English. UNSSC’s International Youth Day announcement also identifies French and Arabic versions. Duration and deadline The course is self-paced. Enrolment closes on December 30, 2026. Access the Children and Armed Conflict Primer How to Register for the UNSSC Courses The exact access route may differ slightly by course, but the general process is: Open the official course page. Review the course description, target audience, duration and deadline. Select the registration or sign-up option. Complete the required registration information. Log in to an existing UNSSC account or create a new account when required. Check the email address used during registration for access instructions. Open the relevant learning platform. Begin the self-paced course. Complete all required modules, quizzes and evaluation activities. Some programmes are hosted on the UNSSC E-Lounge, while Systems Change x Behavioural Science for Climate Action is hosted through UN Learn after the initial UNSSC registration. Participants should check their spam or junk folder if access instructions do not appear in their inbox. UNSSC specifically advises learners to whitelist relevant automated UNSSC email addresses for the Digital4Sustainability Learning Path. Important Points Before Enrolling Registration does not necessarily mean completion Learners should allow enough time to complete the modules before the 2026 course cycle closes. Certificate availability varies The Systems Change x Behavioural Science for Climate Action page expressly confirms a certificate upon completion of its modules, mandatory quiz and evaluation. Learners should not assume that every other course provides a certificate unless the relevant course platform confirms it. Course languages differ Not every course is offered in every language. Learners should select the relevant language version where available. Duration is an estimate The published duration generally refers to the estimated learning time. Applied exercises, reflection and project work may require additional time. There is no application fee All 10 courses covered in this article are officially listed as free. Most courses are open to everyone Although individual courses identify particular target audiences, the official pages generally classify their access as open to everyone. Conclusion The 10 free UNSSC online courses for 2026 provide a valuable opportunity for learners worldwide to develop practical knowledge in some of the most important areas affecting international development and global cooperation. The collection covers the use of technology for sustainability, sustainable consumption, climate leadership, disaster risk reduction, human security, credible environmental marketing, youth participation in peacebuilding, safe engagement at the United Nations and the protection of children affected by conflict. All courses are free and delivered online, with most offering flexible, self-paced learning. Depending on the programme, learners may complete the training in as little as two hours or pursue a broader 12-hour learning path. Enrolment for five courses closes on December 30, 2026, while the remaining five close on December 31, 2026. Interested learners should register early, carefully review completion requirements and allocate sufficient time to finish their chosen courses. For more opportunities, click HERE . title: MORE HEALTH for Africa Program (MH4A) Cohort 3: Up to €80,000 in Catalytic Funding for Healthcare Innovation in Africa
summary: The MORE HEALTH for Africa Program (MH4A) Cohort 3 is now seeking innovative social enterprises working to transform healthcare access and improve health outcomes across Africa. The initiative brings together Boehringer Ingelheim and Villgro Africa to support high-impact healthcare ventures with funding, business development support, investor connections, mentorship, capacity building and opportunities for international exposure. For healthcare-focused social enterprises that have already established their operations and are looking to expand their reach, strengthen their business models and attract significant investment, the MORE HEALTH for Africa Program offers a comprehensive platform for growth. The program is designed around the broader goal of supporting sustainable healthcare solutions that can reach underserved communities while creating measurable and lasting social impact across the continent. What Is the MORE HEALTH for Africa Program? The MORE HEALTH for Africa Program (MH4A) is an initiative established through a partnership between Boehringer Ingelheim and Villgro Africa . Its focus is on supporting social entrepreneurs who are developing innovative approaches to healthcare challenges in Africa. According to Villgro Africa, the program contributes to Boehringer Ingelheim s sustainability commitment to improve the lives of 50 million people through social engagement models by 2030 . Rather than offering funding alone, the program combines financial support with incubation, acceleration, mentorship, business development and access to strategic networks. This integrated approach is intended to help participating enterprises move beyond the early stages of development and build stronger, more scalable healthcare businesses. The third cohort therefore represents an opportunity for established healthcare-focused social enterprises to receive support as they prepare for their next stage of growth. Why the MORE HEALTH for Africa Program Matters Africa continues to face significant healthcare access and delivery challenges, particularly among underserved populations. Social enterprises can play an important role in addressing these challenges by developing innovative products, services, technologies and delivery models. However, promising healthcare enterprises often face barriers when attempting to scale, including limited access to capital, insufficient business infrastructure, challenges with market expansion and difficulty connecting with appropriate investors and strategic partners. The MORE HEALTH for Africa Program seeks to address some of these challenges by combining: Catalytic funding Business development support Mentorship and coaching Capacity-building opportunities Investor linkages Research support Networking opportunities International exposure Peer-to-peer learning This means participants can work on both the internal strength of their organizations and their external growth strategy. What Selected Enterprises Can Receive Successful participants in the MORE HEALTH for Africa Program will have access to a range of financial and non-financial benefits. 1. Catalytic Funding of Up to €80,000 One of the major features of the program is the availability of catalytic grants of up to €80,000 . This funding can provide important financial support to enterprises working to strengthen their operations and expand their impact. Catalytic funding can be particularly valuable for social enterprises because it can help bridge the gap between an organization s current capacity and the resources required to achieve its next growth milestone. The program therefore goes beyond conventional training by providing financial resources alongside business development support. 2. Tailored Business Support Participants will receive support designed around the needs of their individual enterprises. The program aims to help businesses strengthen their models and connect with relevant partners. This tailored approach recognizes that social enterprises at the growth stage may have different challenges depending on their market, operating model, healthcare solution and expansion objectives. Support can therefore help participating enterprises identify weaknesses, improve their strategies and establish stronger foundations for sustainable growth. 3. Investor Linkages Access to appropriate investors can be critical for healthcare enterprises seeking to scale. The program provides opportunities for participating enterprises to connect with potential investors and develop relationships that may support future fundraising. These investor linkages can also help founders better understand investment expectations, improve their investment readiness and position their enterprises for larger funding opportunities. 4. Capacity Building and Masterclasses Participants will also benefit from capacity-building activities, including: Masterclasses Diagnostic panels Research support Business coaching Specialized mentorship These activities are intended to strengthen the skills, systems and strategic capabilities required to manage a growing social enterprise. 5. Global Exposure The program also provides an opportunity for selected enterprises to showcase their work internationally. Participating enterprises can receive exposure through the annual Making More Health Together (MMHT) convention in Germany , as well as one event on the African continent. This exposure can help participating founders introduce their solutions to a wider audience, build relationships with international stakeholders and increase visibility within the global healthcare innovation ecosystem. 6. Peer Learning and Founder Networks Another important component is access to a network of founders from current and previous cohorts within the Villgro Africa portfolio. Peer learning can allow entrepreneurs to exchange experiences, discuss common challenges and learn from other founders who are navigating similar growth journeys. Building these relationships can also create opportunities for future partnerships and collaboration. How the MORE HEALTH for Africa Program Is Structured The program is divided into two major phases: Business Foundations Business Growth Each phase lasts approximately six months, creating a total program structure of about 12 months . Phase One: Business Foundations The first phase, known as Business Foundations , runs for six months. This stage focuses on strengthening the internal foundations of participating enterprises. Before an organization can successfully scale, it needs strong systems, an effective business model, capable leadership and appropriate governance structures. During this phase, participants can work on areas such as: Refining their business models Strengthening organizational structures Building effective teams Improving governance Identifying critical internal gaps Developing stronger operational foundations Participants will also receive coaching and masterclasses designed to address their specific business needs. Tailored grants are another component of this phase, allowing enterprises to address some of their most pressing internal requirements. The objective is to ensure that participating enterprises have stronger foundations from which they can pursue sustainable expansion. Phase Two: Business Growth The second six-month phase is focused on Business Growth . While the first phase concentrates primarily on strengthening the enterprise internally, the Business Growth phase shifts attention toward external opportunities and scaling. Participants can receive support in areas including: Market access Investment readiness Fundraising Business expansion Scaling healthcare solutions Investor engagement Research Global networking Advanced mentorship and investor connections are expected to play an important role during this stage. Research vouchers and networking opportunities can also help enterprises develop stronger evidence, understand their markets and identify opportunities for expansion. Building Investment Readiness For growing social enterprises, preparing for investment is often as important as identifying potential investors. The MORE HEALTH for Africa Program places emphasis on helping enterprises become more prepared to engage with investors. Investment readiness can involve strengthening the business model, improving financial and operational systems, clarifying the growth strategy and demonstrating the potential for measurable impact. Through mentorship, investor linkages and business-development support, the program can help participating enterprises position themselves for future fundraising. Supporting Healthcare Solutions for Underserved Communities At the heart of the program is the goal of expanding access to sustainable healthcare. The initiative is particularly focused on social enterprises capable of addressing healthcare challenges while creating measurable social impact. This makes the program relevant to organizations developing solutions that can improve how healthcare is accessed, delivered or scaled across African communities. The broader objective is not simply to grow individual companies, but to support enterprises whose growth can translate into meaningful improvements in people s lives. International and Continental Networking Opportunities Participation in the program can also provide opportunities to engage with stakeholders beyond the enterprise s immediate market. The opportunity to showcase at the Making More Health Together convention in Germany can provide international visibility, while participation in an event on the African continent can strengthen regional connections. These opportunities can expose entrepreneurs to: Potential partners Investors Healthcare stakeholders Fellow entrepreneurs Innovation networks International organizations Business-development opportunities For enterprises seeking to expand beyond their current markets, such networks can become valuable assets. Peer Learning Through the Villgro Africa Network The program also connects participants with founders from existing and previous Villgro Africa cohorts. This peer network can provide practical learning that complements formal mentorship and masterclasses. Entrepreneurs can potentially learn from the experiences of other founders regarding: Scaling operations Raising capital Entering new markets Managing teams Developing partnerships Building sustainable business models Measuring social impact For founders facing similar challenges, peer learning can provide practical perspectives that are difficult to obtain through conventional training alone. Why Entrepreneurs Should Consider Applying The MORE HEALTH for Africa Program combines several forms of support that are important for enterprises moving into a significant growth phase. Instead of receiving a grant without additional assistance, selected enterprises can benefit from a combination of funding, mentorship, business development, investor access, capacity building, research support and networking . This integrated model can be particularly valuable for enterprises that have already demonstrated their potential and now need additional resources and strategic support to reach a larger number of people. The program can potentially help participating enterprises: Strengthen their business foundations Improve their organizational structures Develop stronger growth strategies Increase investment readiness Connect with investors Access additional research support Expand market opportunities Develop strategic partnerships Increase visibility Learn from other social entrepreneurs Scale healthcare solutions to more communities Application Process Interested enterprises should review the official MORE HEALTH for Africa Program information and submit their application through the designated online application platform. The official Villgro Africa announcement provides an Apply Here link that directs applicants to the program s online application system. Applicants should carefully review the application requirements before submitting their information and ensure that all requested organizational, financial, impact and growth information is accurate and complete. APPLY HERE Deadline No application deadline is stated on the official Villgro Africa funding-call page provided for MORE HEALTH for Africa Program (MH4A) Cohort 3. Applicants should therefore check the official application platform for the current closing date or any deadline updates before applying. Because funding-call timelines can change, prospective applicants are encouraged not to wait until the last moment to begin preparing their applications. How to Prepare a Strong Application Although the program is designed for established social enterprises, applicants should go beyond simply describing their healthcare solution. A strong application should clearly communicate the enterprise s ability to create measurable impact and achieve sustainable growth. Key areas to prepare include: Demonstrate the Healthcare Problem Clearly explain the healthcare challenge being addressed. Describe the communities affected by the problem and explain why the existing healthcare system or available solutions are insufficient. Explain the Solution Clearly demonstrate how the enterprise s product, service or business model addresses the identified healthcare challenge. Applicants should make it easy for reviewers to understand what makes the solution innovative and why it has potential to scale. Demonstrate Impact Use credible evidence to demonstrate the enterprise s existing social impact. Where possible, quantify the number of people reached, communities served and measurable improvements generated by the solution. Present a Strong Business Model Applicants should be able to explain how their enterprise generates revenue and how the business can remain financially sustainable as it grows. Explain the Growth Strategy A strong growth strategy should clearly demonstrate where the enterprise is going next. Explain the markets, customers, partnerships, operational improvements and investment required to achieve the next stage of growth. Show Investment Potential Enterprises seeking to attract substantial future investment should demonstrate why investors would consider the business attractive. This includes communicating the size of the opportunity, market demand, business performance, growth potential and strategic advantages. Demonstrate Team Strength A capable and committed team is essential for scaling a social enterprise. Applicants should clearly communicate the experience, expertise and responsibilities of key members of the leadership team. Key Details at a Glance Program: MORE HEALTH for Africa Program (MH4A) – Cohort 3 Focus: Healthcare innovation and social entrepreneurship Geographic focus: Africa Program partners: Boehringer Ingelheim and Villgro Africa Funding: Catalytic grants of up to €80,000 Program structure: Business Foundations and Business Growth Duration: Six months for each phase Total structured period: Approximately 12 months Business support: Coaching, masterclasses and tailored support Investor support: Investor linkages and investment-readiness assistance Research support: Research assistance and research vouchers Networking: African and international networking opportunities Global exposure: Making More Health Together convention in Germany and an event on the African continent Peer learning: Access to founders from current and previous Villgro Africa cohorts Application deadline: Not stated on the official Villgro Africa funding-call page Visit HERE to learn more about the MORE HEALTH for Africa Program (MH4A) Cohort 3 Conclusion The MORE HEALTH for Africa Program (MH4A) Cohort 3 presents a comprehensive opportunity for healthcare-focused social enterprises seeking to move from established operations to greater scale and impact. With up to €80,000 in catalytic funding , tailored business support, investor linkages, masterclasses, research assistance, mentorship, international exposure and peer learning, the program offers more than financial assistance. It provides a structured environment in which enterprises can strengthen their foundations, improve investment readiness and develop strategies for sustainable growth. The two-stage structure is particularly significant because it addresses both the internal and external needs of a growing enterprise. The Business Foundations phase focuses on strengthening organizational capacity, business models, teams and governance, while the Business Growth phase concentrates on market access, fundraising, investment readiness, networking and scaling. For social enterprises working to expand healthcare access and create measurable impact across Africa, the MORE HEALTH for Africa Program can provide valuable financial, strategic and networking support. Interested applicants should review the official program information carefully and submit their application through the designated online application platform. Since the official Villgro Africa page does not currently state a closing date, applicants should verify the application platform for the latest deadline and program instructions before submitting their application. title: The Open Notebook Early-Career Fellowship Program: Paid Remote Fellowship for Science Journalists Worldwide
summary: The Open Notebook (TON) offers a paid, remote, part-time fellowship program for early-career science journalists who want to strengthen their reporting, interviewing, writing, and storytelling skills while gaining practical experience in professional science journalism. During the year-long fellowship, participants work closely with experienced science-journalism mentors to develop story ideas, report and write articles for publication at The Open Notebook , receive editorial guidance, and become part of TON s wider editorial and fellowship community. For the 2026 fellowship period described by The Open Notebook, the program ran for 12 months , was conducted remotely and part-time, and offered a $6,600 stipend . The scheduled start date was February 23, 2026 . However, prospective applicants should pay close attention to the application status. Applications for the 2026 fellowship period are now closed. The Open Notebook states that it expects applications for the 2027 fellowship to open by late September 2026. Applicants interested in the next cycle should therefore monitor The Open Notebook for the announcement of the 2027 application deadline. This detailed guide explains how The Open Notebook Early-Career Fellowship works, what fellows do, the expected time commitment, eligibility requirements, selection criteria, application materials, and other important information prospective applicants should understand. About The Open Notebook Early-Career Fellowship Program The Open Notebook s Early-Career Fellowship is designed to help emerging science journalists develop professionally through practical reporting, writing, editing, mentoring, and participation in an established science-journalism community. Rather than functioning solely as a classroom-style training program, the fellowship places participants in a real editorial environment. Fellows work with mentors to plan, report, write, revise, and prepare articles for publication by The Open Notebook. The program lasts for one year and is conducted remotely on a part-time basis. The fellowship is supported by the Burroughs Wellcome Fund , which The Open Notebook says has supported the program since 2013. For journalists at an early stage of their careers, this structure provides an opportunity to develop their craft while building published work and professional relationships within the science-journalism community. The Open Notebook Fellowship at a Glance The key details provided for the 2026 fellowship cycle were: Program duration: 12 months Working arrangement: Part-time Location: Remote 2026 fellowship start date: February 23, 2026 Stipend: $6,600 2026 application deadline: October 31, 2025 Current application status: Closed Expected opening of 2027 applications: By late September 2026 Applicants should understand that October 31, 2025 is not the deadline for the upcoming 2027 fellowship . It was the deadline for applications to the 2026 fellowship period. The deadline for the 2027 cycle was not provided in the supplied information. What Fellows Do During the Program The fellowship centers on practical journalism. During the remote, part-time program, fellows pitch, report, and write articles intended for publication by The Open Notebook. The work includes a mixture of story behind the story interviews and reported features , allowing fellows to explore how journalism is produced while simultaneously improving their own reporting and writing skills. An important part of the program is the relationship between each fellow and an experienced science journalist serving as a mentor. One-on-One Mentorship Fellows have weekly phone or video meetings with their mentors . Mentors help fellows: Develop and refine potential story ideas; Shape stories into workable projects; Improve reporting techniques; Strengthen writing; Review and edit article drafts; Navigate the reporting and revision process; Develop their understanding of the craft of science journalism; and Think about broader professional and career-development questions. The mentoring component therefore extends beyond correcting individual articles. It is designed to help fellows become stronger journalists and make more informed decisions as they develop their careers. Become Part of The Open Notebook Editorial Community The fellowship also provides a community element. Fellows and mentors participate in a Slack discussion group that includes current and former fellowship participants as well as editors from The Open Notebook. Fellows participate in cohort-based activities through this Slack community during the fellowship. Importantly, membership in the community continues after the fellowship ends . This can be particularly valuable for early-career journalists because professional development often depends not only on technical skills but also on access to peers, experienced journalists, editors, feedback, and professional relationships. How Much Work Does the Fellowship Require? Although the fellowship is part-time, applicants should not assume that the workload is minimal. The Open Notebook estimates that most fellows spend approximately five to seven hours per week on average completing fellowship-related responsibilities. However, this is an estimate rather than a fixed weekly workload. The amount of time required can vary depending on: A fellow s previous journalism experience; Individual working and writing style; The complexity of a particular article; Whether the fellow is researching, reporting, writing, revising, or fact-checking at a particular point in the process; and The number and complexity of revisions required. Some weeks may consequently require more than five to seven hours, while others may require less. Fellows Are Expected to Produce Four Major Articles A major component of the fellowship is producing four articles of approximately 1,500 to 2,000 words each for The Open Notebook. Producing these stories involves considerably more than simply drafting four pieces. Fellows are expected to participate in the broader reporting and editorial process, which may include: Developing story ideas; Researching proposed subjects; Conducting interviews; Reporting stories; Writing drafts; Receiving editorial feedback; Completing multiple rounds of revisions; Annotating stories for fact-checking; Meeting article deadlines; and Preparing work for eventual publication. The program therefore requires sustained engagement throughout the year. Applicants Should Carefully Consider the Weekly Commitment The Open Notebook specifically warns prospective applicants that balancing the fellowship with other commitments can be challenging. Successful fellows must be able to make sufficient time for the program and meet deadlines consistently. Among other responsibilities, participants should expect to make time for: Phone interviews with sources, which ordinarily take place during U.S. daytime hours; Weekly telephone or video meetings with their mentors; Multiple rounds of editing and revision for most articles; Story annotation as part of fact-checking; and Participation in conversations and activities within the fellowship Slack community. This consideration may be particularly important for applicants combining the fellowship with full-time employment, graduate studies, dissertations, freelance work, family responsibilities, or other substantial professional obligations. Eligibility Requirements for The Open Notebook Early-Career Fellowship The fellowship is intended for early-career science journalists . One of its most significant features is its international accessibility. Applicants do not have to live in the United States . The Open Notebook explicitly states that people living outside the U.S. are welcome to apply. This makes the program relevant to emerging science journalists around the world. Some Public-Facing Writing Experience Is Required Applicants must have some training and/or experience in writing for the general public. Extensive professional experience is not required. In fact, the program is specifically designed for journalists who are still relatively early in their careers. However, applicants cannot be completely without relevant experience or training. They need to demonstrate at least some background in public-facing writing. Professional Science-Writing Experience Limit Science journalists and aspiring science journalists should generally have fewer than three years of regular professional science-writing experience . There are important qualifications to this rule. Internships and student work do not count toward the fewer-than-three-years requirement. The Open Notebook may also make exceptions where an applicant has more than three years of professional science-writing experience but some or all of that professional experience was not in English . This provision can make the program more accessible to journalists who developed professionally in another language before moving into English-language science journalism. English-Language Requirements Applications must be submitted in English. This requirement extends to: Application responses; Writing samples; and Letters of recommendation. However, materials that were originally produced in another language may be translated into English and submitted. The selection criteria also indicate that applicants whose first language is not English are not expected to demonstrate flawless English writing. Nevertheless, participants need a sufficiently high level of English proficiency to work effectively within the fellowship s reporting, writing, editing, mentoring, and publication process. What The Open Notebook Looks for When Selecting Fellows Meeting the basic eligibility requirements does not automatically make an applicant competitive. The Open Notebook identifies several qualities that receive priority during selection. 1. Serious Interest in Professional Science Journalism Applicants should demonstrate a strong intention to work primarily as professional science journalists . This distinction is important. The fellowship is specifically focused on journalism rather than the much broader field of science communication. Applicants should therefore be able to demonstrate that journalism itself is central to their professional goals. 2. Experience Writing About Science for the Public Candidates should have at least some training or experience communicating science through writing intended for a general audience. The experience does not need to be extensive. 3. Understanding of the Science-Journalism Profession Strong candidates should demonstrate some awareness of: How science journalism works; Challenges commonly encountered by science journalists; Skills they currently possess; Areas in which they need additional development; and How the fellowship could help them grow professionally. Applicants should therefore approach the application as an opportunity to demonstrate both existing knowledge and a thoughtful understanding of their own development needs. 4. Familiarity With The Open Notebook Candidates should familiarize themselves with The Open Notebook and the kinds of stories it publishes . This becomes particularly important because applicants are required to propose potential TON stories as part of the application. A generic journalism proposal that does not fit The Open Notebook s editorial focus is unlikely to demonstrate the same preparation as a proposal clearly developed with the publication in mind. 5. Ability to Generate Strong Story Ideas Applicants should demonstrate that they can develop interesting and appropriate story ideas suitable for The Open Notebook. Story ideation is therefore an important part of the selection process. 6. Reliability and Commitment to Deadlines The program emphasizes conscientiousness and the ability to deliver high-quality work on schedule. Because fellows go through a rigorous editorial process involving reporting, writing, editing, revisions, fact-checking, and publication, reliability is an important professional requirement. 7. Strong Writing Ability Writing ability is another selection factor. Applicants whose first language is not English should note that The Open Notebook says it takes this into consideration and does not expect flawless English. However, participants need enough English proficiency to successfully complete a demanding English-language journalism fellowship. Required Application Materials The fellowship application requires several components. Prospective candidates can strengthen their preparation by understanding these requirements well before applications open. 1. Responses to Application Questions Applicants are asked to respond to questions addressing topics including: Why they are interested in the fellowship; What they hope to learn from participating; Previous training and/or experience writing science stories for the general public; Particular skills, interests, or perspectives they could bring to the fellowship; and Their broader plans during the fellowship period. The final area is particularly important because The Open Notebook wants to understand what other commitments applicants may have during the fellowship. For example, an applicant may simultaneously be: Completing a dissertation; Freelancing; Looking for full-time employment; Studying; Working elsewhere; or Managing another major professional commitment. Candidates should answer these questions carefully and accurately, particularly given the fellowship s significant time requirements. 2. Two Short Story Proposals Applicants must submit two short proposals for potential The Open Notebook features or multimedia stories . These should be ideas suitable for publication by TON. Possible formats include: Behind-the-story interviews with writers; Reported features examining an aspect of the craft of science writing; Roundtable discussions; or Other creative feature-length projects focused on the craft of science writing. Each proposal is approximately 100 words . These are brief proposals rather than complete, full-scale pitches. Because applicants are specifically evaluated partly on their familiarity with The Open Notebook and their ability to generate appropriate story ideas, prospective candidates should spend time reading TON before developing their proposals. 3. Resume or CV Applicants must provide a resume or curriculum vitae (CV) . The document should enable reviewers to understand the applicant s educational, writing, journalism, employment, training, and other relevant professional background. 4. One Letter of Reference Applicants need one reference letter . The reference may come from an appropriate person such as a: Professor; Editor; Mentor; Supervisor; or Professional colleague. Applicants should select someone capable of speaking meaningfully about their skills and personal or professional qualities as they relate to science journalism and participation in the fellowship. Candidates should also contact their prospective referee early rather than waiting until the final days of the application process. 5. Up to Two Writing or Multimedia Samples Candidates can submit up to two writing or multimedia samples intended for the general public. Scientific or academic writing is not appropriate for this requirement. For audio or multimedia work, applicants may place URLs linking to the work into a PDF and upload that document. Samples must be available in English, although translated work is accepted. Applicants should therefore select examples that demonstrate their ability to communicate effectively with general audiences rather than submitting highly technical academic publications simply because those pieces concern science. 6. Optional Background Information The application also provides candidates with an optional opportunity to share additional information about themselves. The Open Notebook states that it strongly encourages writers from all types of backgrounds to apply. Applicants who belong to groups or communities historically marginalized or underrepresented in U.S. journalism are invited to provide that information if they wish. Disclosure is entirely optional , and The Open Notebook states that information disclosed in this section is kept confidential. Application Deadline for the 2026 Fellowship For the 2026 fellowship cycle, applications had to be received by: 11:59 p.m. U.S. Central Time on October 31, 2025. The reference-letter deadline was later: November 7, 2025. Applicants were advised to notify their letter writers well ahead of the deadline so referees would have sufficient time to prepare thoughtful recommendations. These deadlines have now passed. What About the 2027 Fellowship Deadline? Prospective applicants should distinguish between the completed 2026 application cycle and the upcoming 2027 cycle. The Open Notebook states that applications for the 2026 fellowship period have closed and that it expects to open applications for the 2027 fellowship by late September 2026 . The supplied program information does not provide the 2027 application deadline . Therefore, prospective 2027 applicants should not assume that October 31 will automatically be the next deadline. They should check the official 2027 fellowship announcement once applications open for the confirmed closing date and any updated program requirements. How Prospective 2027 Applicants Can Prepare Although the next application period has not yet opened according to the supplied information, prospective candidates can use the time before the launch to prepare. Step 1: Read The Open Notebook Extensively Candidates should become familiar with TON s editorial approach and the subjects it covers. This preparation can help applicants understand what constitutes an appropriate story idea and make their two short proposals substantially more relevant. Step 2: Review Your Professional Experience Applicants should determine whether they satisfy the early-career experience requirement, particularly the guideline concerning fewer than three years of regular professional science-writing experience. Remember that internships and student work are excluded from that calculation. Step 3: Select Potential Work Samples Review previously published or completed public-facing journalism and identify up to two strong samples. Candidates whose strongest work was originally published in another language can consider preparing English translations because translated materials are permitted. Step 4: Identify a Strong Referee Consider who can provide the most meaningful assessment of your potential as a science journalist. The best referee is not necessarily the person with the most prestigious title. A professor, editor, supervisor, mentor, or colleague who knows your work well may be better positioned to provide a detailed recommendation. Step 5: Develop Potential TON Story Ideas Because two short proposals form part of the application, candidates can begin observing recurring questions, challenges, techniques, and emerging issues in the craft of science journalism. Ideas can then be evaluated against the kinds of stories The Open Notebook actually publishes. Step 6: Assess Your Availability Before applying, consider whether you can realistically commit to the fellowship for an entire year. The estimated five-to-seven-hour average weekly workload should not be interpreted as a guaranteed maximum. Reporting deadlines, revisions, interviews, and fact-checking may make particular weeks significantly busier. Why This Fellowship Can Be Valuable for Early-Career Science Journalists The structure of The Open Notebook Early-Career Fellowship brings together several forms of professional development that emerging journalists often need simultaneously. Fellows receive: Practical reporting assignments; Publication opportunities; One-on-one mentorship; Editorial guidance; Repeated feedback and revision experience; Exposure to professional fact-checking processes; Experience developing and pitching story ideas; Participation in an editorial community; Contact with current and former fellows; Career-development guidance; and Financial support through the fellowship stipend. The combination of mentoring and actual publication work is particularly significant. Fellows are not simply learning about journalism in theory; they are expected to practice the reporting, writing, revision, and deadline-management processes required in professional journalism. Important Considerations Before Applying Prospective applicants should carefully consider several questions before submitting an application: Do I genuinely intend to pursue journalism? The program prioritizes applicants who want professional science journalism, rather than other forms of science communication, to be their primary professional direction. Do I have enough relevant experience to qualify? Applicants need some training or experience writing for the general public, even though extensive experience is not required. Am I still within the early-career experience range? Applicants should review the fewer-than-three-years professional science-writing guideline and its stated exceptions. Can I work effectively in English? Perfect English is not expected from applicants who speak it as an additional language, but sufficient proficiency is necessary to participate successfully. Can I make time for the program? Five to seven hours per week is an average estimate, and some periods can demand considerably more time. Can I reliably meet deadlines? Fellows need to complete stories, revisions, fact-checking preparations, meetings, and other responsibilities according to schedule. Do I understand The Open Notebook? Familiarity with the publication is an explicit selection consideration and is particularly important when developing the two proposed story ideas. APPLY NOW Conclusion The The Open Notebook Early-Career Fellowship Program offers emerging science journalists an opportunity to develop professional skills through a combination of mentorship, reporting, writing, editing, publication, and community participation. The remote, part-time structure makes the fellowship accessible to applicants beyond the United States, while its focus on early-career journalists provides developing writers with an opportunity to learn directly from experienced science-journalism professionals. For the 2026 fellowship period, the program offered a $6,600 stipend , lasted 12 months , began on February 23, 2026 , and required an estimated average commitment of approximately five to seven hours per week . The 2026 application deadline was October 31, 2025, at 11:59 p.m. U.S. Central Time , with reference letters due November 7, 2025. That application cycle is now closed. The next important date for prospective applicants is therefore the expected opening of the 2027 fellowship application cycle by late September 2026 . Since the supplied information does not specify the 2027 deadline, prospective applicants should monitor The Open Notebook s official fellowship information for the new application announcement and confirmed deadline. In the meantime, potential candidates can prepare by reading The Open Notebook s journalism, developing appropriate story ideas, identifying strong work samples and a suitable referee, reviewing their eligibility, and ensuring they can make the substantial year-long commitment the fellowship requires. For aspiring and early-career science journalists seeking structured mentorship, professional editorial experience, published work, and deeper involvement in the international science-journalism community, The Open Notebook Early-Career Fellowship is an opportunity worth preparing for well before the next application window opens. If you have any questions, please email TON executive director and editor-in-chief Siri Carpenter: siricarpenter@theopennotebook.com . Visit the OFY website for more Fellowship Opportunities .
